top.line: Versions signed off by their maintainers, buyers who require it, and money flowing down the chain, scaled by Gen AI.
top.para: A follow-up to the maintenance deficit, solutions first. Platform versions should be signed off by their maintainers, the town planners, who support and patch them and push quality downstream. Buyers should require that signature, sending money down the chain, with links to insurance and a licence to operate. Small purchases in proportion; Gen AI scales it.

in-short.line: The proposal: sign-off, the town planners, buyers require it, money down the chain, proportion, Gen AI, risk.
in-short.para: Maintainers sign off the builds they stand behind and support them; they are the town planners, pushing quality downstream, with certification insurers and regulators can rely on. Buyers require the signature, so money flows down the chain. Maintenance is many small purchases sized to each project, adding value. Gen AI scales understanding and support. No signature is a mapped risk.

the-case.line: Open source as smaller, customised, maintained versions, with a direct line to maintainers; RiskMandate sells it.
the-case.para: On open-source.sgit.ai I argue that open source's value is in customised, maintainable, smaller versions: customisation is subtraction, and the maintainer is the package. The missing piece is the connection between maintainers and users. RiskMandate, which I co-founded, builds every customer version on the open base, so I have a commercial interest. php2shell shows the market already exists.

signed-off.line: A cryptographic sign-off by the people who maintain a platform, on the version a product ships, required by buyers.
signed-off.para: The key authors of a technology sign the specific build a product ships, stand behind it, and help set up, support and patch it. PHP has signed release tags since 2012; a signed customer version with support is the missing step. Buyers refusing products without that signature create a financial flow down the chain and an ecosystem of assurance providers.

town-planners.line: PHP's maintainers are its town planners: paid to read, maintain and sign off code, pushing quality downstream.
town-planners.para: In explorer-coding terms, explorers build, villagers maintain and town planners own production code; PHP's maintainers are its town planners. The Linux kernel already requires human sign-off. Signing means refusing what they do not support, which pushes quality downstream. A certified application is a risk insurers can price, and for critical services sign-off could become a licence to operate.

gen-ai.line: Gen AI scales the work around the code, understanding, support and side effects, not by writing all the code.
gen-ai.para: This is not Gen AI writing the code or sitting in the middle; the maintainers still read the code, which is what they sign. Gen AI helps understand code bases, side effects, architectures and changes, and scales the non-functional work, so mass-customised support can be sold at a price that makes sense, with experts covering far more versions.

proportional.line: Many small purchases in proportion to each project's spend, adding value all the time, never insurance.
proportional.para: Maintaining an application's core software should cost in proportion to the money in that project, through many small purchases rather than one large one. It must show value monthly, or it gets cut as insurance. Its absence is a risk, and the data to map it exists: 751 products in the NCSC inventory, 295 sites dark.

two-questions.line: Either a switched-off site does not matter, or it matters and someone must pay to maintain it; measure the cost.
two-questions.para: Sites went offline because nobody could quickly say they were safe, since nobody was paid to know. No named source has estimated the php2shell shutdown costs; for Log4j, one US federal department reported 33,000 hours of response. Each organisation could count its own hours offline, affected users and staff time: the budget its maintenance should have had.

both-ways.line: Buyers cannot buy maintenance of what they run; the PHP Foundation sells sponsorship logos; the packager works in their free time.
both-ways.para: Organisations running PHP budget for building, migrating and hosting, but cannot buy maintenance of their exact stack, so they switch sites off. The PHP Foundation sells sponsorship tiers from $12,000 a year with logos and an advisory seat, not support or maintained builds. The Debian and Ubuntu packager works mostly in their free time. Money stops with integrators.

old-versions.line: The security team published free source backports; Zend, Ubuntu, TuxCare, HeroDevs and Freexian sold builds; none states a share back.
old-versions.para: PHP 8.1 and older get no project releases, but the security team published free source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. Vendors sold ready-made fixes almost at once. Only Zend appears among the Foundation's sponsors, at the Silver tier, and no vendor states a revenue share to PHP. The fixes were written by a donation-funded team and resold.

openjs.line: OpenJS's partner programme is the best that exists today, and not what should happen.
openjs.para: Since May 2024 OpenJS endorses partners selling fixes for end-of-life versions, and HeroDevs shares 15% of revenue with participating projects. It is the best available now, but it keeps maintainers at one remove. The proposal is more direct: a commercial decision by everyone who depends on the code, with the maintainers' own signature. Tidelift, the Pledge and Sponsors point similarly.

experts.line: PHP's own developers are the best maintainers, but no workflow lets a buyer hire them for what it runs.
experts.para: Core developers and those around the Foundation know which fixes and back-ports are safe, yet a council or company cannot buy their maintenance of its PHP. From commercial experience, a maintainer tied to the source and serving many customers invests in scalable processes, tooling and tests that benefit everyone; a consultancy patching one site does not.

services.line: Seven services: bring sites back, maintained builds, patching on behalf, code removal, a dependency register, an incident desk, endorsed partners.
services.para: Restore switched-off sites with reach mapping and patching, priced per site. Sell minimal, back-ported, signed PHP builds. Patch the CMS and plugins on each customer's copy. Remove unused code, easier in interpreted PHP. Keep a register of dependency, usage and maintainability that executives sign. Offer fast evidence-based assessment. Endorse partners with a revenue share.

selling.line: Paid to map, paid to engineer, a scoped custom version, retained to maintain: RiskMandate's options, applied to PHP.
selling.para: RiskMandate's current proposal maps four ways to make money from open source: mapping one site, engineering the change, a custom version built on the open code, and maintenance priced by how critical the system is. Customers pay for the work, not for access to code, which stays open. Smaller versions are easier to maintain, and improvements can go back to everyone.

regulation.line: Make maintenance easy to buy first, then required through procurement line items and regulation.
regulation.para: Foundations could publish how to become an endorsed maintenance partner and the share paid. Procurement could ask who maintains each open source dependency and how they are paid, with a maintainer line item. Regulation such as the Cyber Resilience Act, which holds manufacturers answerable for open source in products, could recognise endorsed maintenance as meeting that duty.

beyond.line: The same holds for Node, Python and every runtime; this is about fixing open source's economics, not leaving it.
beyond.para: PHP is this week's example, but every runtime and library faces the same questions: what we depend on, how much we use it, who maintains it, and how they are paid. JavaScript has a revenue-sharing model and Python a supported security role; most projects have neither. The aim is to pay the people who keep the code safe.

limits.line: Proposals throughout: services, sign-off, prices, insurance and licence links; plus data caveats and my interest.
limits.para: The services, the signed-off version, RiskMandate's prices, and links to insurance and a licence to operate are proposals. Not shown as a sponsor refers to the home page; no stated share is not no share. Some fix dates are unconfirmed and no shutdown cost exists. Gen AI scales the work around the code, not replacing the maintainers. I have a commercial interest.

sources.line: My memo, php.net, the Foundation, vendors, OpenJS, open-source.sgit.ai and RiskMandate's current proposal.
sources.para: My voice memo of 23 October; php.net's advisory; the PHP Foundation and its sponsorship tiers; Zend, Ubuntu, TuxCare, HeroDevs, Freexian and deb.sury.org; the OpenJS announcement; Tidelift, the Open Source Pledge and GitHub Sponsors; open-source.sgit.ai's pages on packaging, funding and the villagers; RiskMandate's current commercial proposal; and the Log4j review board report.
